definition: Deferential means showing respect for another person's authority, rank, or greater experience.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word deferential. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know deferential should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The young lawyer was deferential toward the retired judge, standing when she entered and weighing her every suggestion with care.
Polite behavior shows ordinary good manners to anyone at all, while deferential behavior specifically acknowledges another person's higher rank or greater experience.
A deferential junior still keeps her own judgment while honoring a superior's, but a servile one surrenders it entirely, obeying every instruction without question.

Respectful means showing due regard for another person - any person, in any direction: adults can be respectful to children, rivals to each other. Deferential is respect with a direction built in: it flows upward, acknowledging that the other person's rank or experience outranks yours. You can be respectful to an equal; you defer to a superior.

Reverent means showing deep, awed respect - the hushed manner reserved for sacred places, solemn ceremonies, and heroes. Deferential is more workaday: it yields to a person's higher rank or seniority in ordinary dealings, standing when the judge enters or letting the veteran speak first. Reverence borders on worship; deference is a professional bow.

Deferential means showing respect for another person's authority, rank, or greater experience.
On his first day in the restaurant kitchen, the culinary school graduate arrived with plenty of his own ideas about the menu.
Still, when the head chef of thirty years demonstrated her way of preparing the sauces, he watched closely, asked permission before suggesting changes, and addressed her as 'Chef' at every turn.
His deferential manner made clear that he recognized her decades of experience outranked his fresh diploma.
The graduate showed respect specifically for the head chef's authority and greater experience, which is exactly what deferential describes.
Deferential usually appears in the patterns 'deferential to' or 'deferential toward' plus the person being honored (deferential to the committee chair).
It is stronger and more specific than polite: deferential behavior acknowledges that the other person holds higher standing, rank, or experience, not merely that they deserve courtesy.

At ninety-one, the conductor Aurelio Marchetti no longer hears the upper strings clearly, and everyone in the orchestra knows it.

Yet at rehearsal the young guest soloist remains deferential: she waits for his downbeat, accepts his slower tempos without protest, and brings her questions to him privately rather than raising them from the stage.
Critics sometimes mistake this for timidity.
The soloist laughs at the idea.
Her manner, she says, is a choice: sixty years on the podium have earned him the benefit of every doubt.
She will argue with him about phrasing — but afterward, in his study, and in the end she lets the old man decide.
